item.title: How to Self-Actualise
item.description:
Identity

How to Self-Actualise

A generalisable process for building a life tailored to you.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Self-actualisation is key to well-being.
  • You need to harmonise your actual, ideal, and ought self.
  • Use affective and social feedback to refine your identity.
  • Introspection is key to getting recalibrations of your goals right.

Self-actualisation is one of the oldest themes of therapy. It is present in all the founders, especially Jung’s notion of individuation, Carl Rogers’ sublime book On Becoming a Person, and Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, with self-actualisation on top. Yet few have ever outlined how to do self-actualisation in any systematic way.

Self-actualisation is a long and hard process but you'll grow into it
Source: Katrina Wright /Unsplash

I have a go at it in my book Beyond Happy, drawing on perspectives from humanistic psychology, existentialist philosophy, and more recent ideas in quantitative psychological science. I’ll sketch my approach here.

A useful place to start is self-discrepancy theory. It argues that we have a sense of three self concepts:

  • Our actual self is who we perceive ourselves to be right now
  • The ideal self is who we would like to be
  • And the ought self is who we feel a responsibility to be.

Begin by developing a thorough understanding of how each of these manifests in you. A journal can help.

Be mindful of what in your ideal and ought self is authentic to you versus a product of your environment or socialisation. The influence of family and trusted peers can be benevolent and beneficial, but you first need to get some distance from it if you want self-discovery.

The next step is self-creation: Bring your actual self into alignment with your ideal self, subject to the constraint imposed by your ought self.

This might require some tricky harmonisation. Consider a young woman who aspires to be a judge on the International Court of Justice. There’s a fast track there through commercial law, but she feels queasy about representing immoral companies. This is her ought self speaking, and harmonisation might require taking a slower route, perhaps through environmental law instead.

Your ideal self doesn’t need to be ambitious; indeed, that might be wholly unsuitable for you. Your ideal self is simply the person you’d be most proud to be. You might want to be a folksy type with lots of spare time to help friends and enjoy an array of hobbies. Stay true to yourself.

Now your first guess at your ideal self is likely to be wrong. Self-actualisation is an iterative process, and you’ll learn by doing.

That learning comes principally in the form of affective feedback. Joy, serenity, exhilaration and other positive emotions are signals to invest more.

What about negative feedback? Self-discrepancy theory finds that depression attends discrepancies between the actual and ideal self, while anxiety is associated with actual-ought self discrepancies. But you need to introspect to understand what these feelings mean for you in each case.

Are you depressed because your ideal self is meaningful to you and you’re not living up to it? Then that negative emotion is a signal to try harder.

But if you’re depressed because achieving your ideal is hard and feels like a drag, that’s a two-part affective signal. There’s depression, but also a lack of enthusiasm.

Here we get our next big self-actualisation puzzle piece from self-determination theory: There are five varieties of motivation running on a spectrum from extrinsic to relatively intrinsic.

Source: Mark Fabian based on Ryan and Deci 2017

Extrinsically motivated activities are done under duress. They require a great deal of self-regulation to enact because you don’t want to do them.

Introjected activities are done for a reason contingent to the activity itself. For example, many people put up with exercise because they want to be healthy.

We’re more autonomous here, but there’s still a lot of self-regulation going on, so these activities tend to drain our willpower and feel exhausting. If there’s no sense of achievement afterwards, then the activity is likely unsustainable.

The depressed and demotivated individual above is probably doing something introjected. The lack of enthusiasm is a signal that it’s not authentic to them.

They should switch to something with intrinsic motivation. These activities are self-determined, which means we do them spontaneously for their own sake. They’re associated with feelings of interest and vitality.

Not everything in the ideal and ought selves will be intrinsically motivated. Indeed, when self-actualisation begins, it usually involves a lot of identified motivation. This is where we value something but don’t have intrinsic motivation for it.

I value being honest, for example, but it didn’t come naturally to me. Indeed, it took at least a decade of deliberate effort to stop telling white lies.

Introjected and identified motivations can be internalised over time until they become intrinsic, but sustaining the necessary effort requires payoffs in the form of frequent positive feedback.

For example, I loathed mathematics in school. But training in it has made me a better social scientist, for which I have intrinsic motivation. Seeing the ways math would help me achieve this part of my ideal self kept me going through my statistics classes. Nowadays maths comes much more easily to me; it’s not a joy, but I don’t notice it enough to loathe it anymore.

This is an example of integrated motivation – where something identified becomes connected to something intrinsically motivated, and so is easier to engage in.

Let me bring this all together in a simple model of self-actualisation, shown in the image below. Imagine a young woman who dreams of being an astronaut. She identifies two activities as central to this ideal self – science and athletics, so she enrols in chemistry and a gymnastics club.

A model of the self-actualisation process
Source: Mark Fabian

As she goes about these activities, she gets feedback. Maybe she likes gymnastics, but this particular club is full of overly competitive people. Introspecting on this feedback, she realises that gymnastics is right for her; she just needs to join a more casual club.

She loves chemistry, but her casual interest in gymnastics means she won’t be fit enough to be an astronaut. She needs to recalibrate her ideal self. Maybe she can be a terrestrial scientist and study samples sent by the astronauts to her lab.

This cycle of goal, feedback, introspection, and recalibration takes place across all facets of your life, slowly bringing them into harmony and yourself into actualisation.

item.title: Five Strategies to Address Acute Insomnia
item.description:
Insomnia

Five Strategies to Address Acute Insomnia

Short-term sleep issues can cause significant distress. Here’s what you can do.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Acute insomnia is defined as having trouble sleeping at least three days a week for up to three months.
  • Acute insomnia often arises after a stressful life event but can become self-perpetuating if prolonged.
  • One study suggests that just one session of CBT-I can improve sleep for folks suffering from acute insomnia.
  • Five CBT-I behavioral strategies, shared here, may help resolve short-term sleep difficulties.
Source: cottonbro studio / Pexels

Even just one night of poor sleep can lead to an unpleasant experience the next day: grogginess, having trouble concentrating, or feeling grumpier than usual. If you have multiple nights of poor sleep in a week, you may be experiencing acute insomnia, and significant worry about sleep may start to creep in.

How Is Acute Insomnia Defined?

Acute insomnia involves having difficulty falling asleep at least three nights per week for a period lasting anywhere between three days and three months. At the three-month mark, insomnia is considered chronic rather than acute and could be diagnosed as an insomnia disorder based on the standards laid out in the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5-TR). At any given time, around 10% of individuals in the United States experience acute insomnia, and approximately one-third of Americans experience a period of acute insomnia in any given year.

Why Does Acute Insomnia Occur?

Sleep is a dynamic, complex, multi-system process, so a whole range of events and issues can lead to difficulty sleeping. A major schedule change, such as working the late shift or overnight, can lead to major sleep issues due to disruptions in circadian rhythms and the sleep-wake cycle. Similarly, experiencing jet lag after crossing time zones, having a baby that is up at all hours of the night, or contracting a new illness or injury can all lead to short-term disruptions in sleep.

Stress also has a strong impact on sleep. The classic stress response, which involves activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, impacts the sleep-wake cycle. Sometimes an initial stress response stems from a life event, such as a job layoff, the breakup of a relationship, or an upcoming high-stakes exam. These stressors can lead to physiological hyperarousal, such as the “fight-or-flight response.” It is difficult to fall asleep when your heart or mind is racing. Over the course of several nights or weeks, difficulty sleeping itself can become a stressor, ironically causing even further sleep disturbance.

Can Acute Insomnia Be Treated Without Medications?

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is considered the first-line treatment for insomnia disorder by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM). Although CBT-I is typically recommended only for folks who have crossed the three-month threshold into chronic insomnia, there is evidence that it may also provide benefit for short-term sleep difficulties. One randomized controlled trial found that a single-session version of CBT-I provided significant improvement for individuals with acute insomnia, with 60% of those in the CBT-I group achieving remission within one month, compared with only 15% in the control group.

CBT-I does not require medication, but it does involve more than traditional sleep hygiene. The treatment combines behavioral components, such as refraining from activities other than sleep in bed, with cognitive components, such as changing your upsetting or self-defeating thoughts about sleep. If you are suffering from acute insomnia, here are five behavioral strategies from CBT-I that may help you shift the tide back to your normal, pre-insomnia sleep pattern.

  1. Keep to a regular morning wake-up time. We sleep best on a set schedule because it allows our bodies to sync with our natural circadian rhythms. Although many people try to go to bed at the same time each night, we can’t actually control when we fall asleep. One of the best ways to regulate circadian rhythm is to wake up at the same time each morning, regardless of how well you slept the night before.
  2. Cut out naps (unless needed for safety purposes). Naps might feel like a clever way to get more sleep in, but they weaken the sleep drive, or our daily need for sleep. Taking an afternoon nap might make it harder for you to fall or stay asleep the next night. However, if you tend to doze or fall asleep during the day, a thirty-minute power nap may be an important safety precaution before driving or operating heavy machinery.
  3. Give yourself at least an hour-long buffer before bed. Calming activities can lower stress levels and signal to your body that sleep is approaching. At least an hour before your typical bedtime, shift towards soothing, calming, or low-energy activities. These could include reading, a nighttime skincare routine, listening to a podcast or audiobook, taking a warm bath, or stretching.
  4. Wait until you are actually sleepy before getting into bed. If you get in bed while wired, you are unlikely to fall asleep quickly. The process of tossing and turning can increase your stress levels or, worse, lead you to start associating the bed with wakefulness. Signs of sleepiness include yawning, heavy eyelids, or even nodding off. If your bedtime comes around and you aren’t sleepy yet, it is better to engage in calming activities until sleepiness sets in rather than trying to “force” sleep.
  5. Get out of bed if you have been lying awake for more than 20 (or so) minutes. Spending long stretches of time in bed without sleeping can create a mental association between the bed and wakefulness, which could increase your risk for developing chronic insomnia. Before you go to bed tonight, identify a comfortable area in your home where you can sit and engage in a quiet activity if you have trouble sleeping. For example, set out a book of crossword puzzles on a couch with a soft blanket and access to lamplight. If you can’t sleep, go to that spot and engage in another activity until you feel sleepy. Then get back in bed, better prepared to drift off.

item.title: Dr. Linehan, You Changed the World
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder

Dr. Linehan, You Changed the World

How one woman changed the way psychiatry views suffering.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • People suffering aren't broken, untreatable, or being difficult.
  • Validation acknowledges painful emotions without endorsing harmful behavior.
  • Two things can be true: I am doing the best I can, and I can do better.
Marsha Linehan as a faculty member at The Catholic University of America in the 1970s.
Source: Dr. Marsha Linehan, used with permission

Back in the early 1990s, I did my undergrad psychology degree. My first-year psychology textbook had a whole chapter on personality disorders. It basically described personality disorders as unchanging, difficult ways of being; this was even how they were classified in the DSM-IV. The textbook didn’t say it directly, but the implication was that if patients didn’t get better as quickly as the psychiatrist wanted them to or didn’t follow the clinician’s instructions, then it was clearly the patient’s fault and they should be labelled as having borderline personality disorder. Patients were considered to be difficult, untreatable, and neurotic. They blamed the patient, even though they also knew that the majority of people diagnosed as BPD had a history of childhood sexual abuse.

In the corner of my first-year textbook chapter, in a little box, there were three paragraphs about a radical alternative theory of borderline personality disorder, developed by US psychologist Dr. Marsha Linehan. She dared to question the mainstream view by suggesting that borderline personality disorder is due to a combination of temperament and an invalidating environment, rather than being the patient's fault. She then even more radically suggested that BPD is treatable, and people who had previously been written off by psychiatrists as being broken for life can go on to live safe, healthy, and meaningful lives.

Extreme suffering doesn't mean untreatable or choosing to be difficult
Source: Image by Khoi Chau /pixels.com

Dr. Linehan developed a specific therapy called dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), which helps people learn a number of skills to live a life worth living. There are distress tolerance skills, which help you safely and calmly get through a rough few minutes despite strong urges to self-harm, pick a fight, or make things worse. There are emotion regulation skills, which are the things that you do long term to help you live on a more even keel and be less likely to need to use your distress tolerance skills. Interpersonal effectiveness skills help you get your needs met and feel heard in ways that don’t inadvertently lead to rejection or more harm. Woven throughout these skills are also mindfulness skills, because if you can’t bring yourself back to where you are right now and can’t recognise how you’re feeling in this moment, then you won’t be able to choose the right skills to help yourself.

I am a DBT-trained therapist, though I’m not currently working in a DBT service. Yet there are therapy skills developed by Dr. Linehan within DBT that I use every day in my practice, and I suspect almost all therapists now use in their practice. For example, she taught me how to validate more effectively in ways that validate the person's emotion, even when the behaviour that followed the emotion wasn’t helpful. Instead of "why did you self-harm?", I might say "it sounds like you were really sad and unsure what to do." More importantly, she brought the idea of dialectics into therapy, where two opposing ideas can both be true; the most crucial one is "I'm doing the best I can, and I can do better.”

So, Dr. Linehan, thank you for developing a theory and a therapy that taught me many specific important skills. But more importantly, thank you for changing the entire psychiatric world so we understand extreme human suffering with more compassion and less patient blaming. Dr. Marsha Linehan, you changed the world.

item.title: The Diary of a Worried Healer
item.description:
Anxiety

The Diary of a Worried Healer

Personal Perspective: A therapist’s experience with generalized anxiety disorder.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Knowing anxiety professionally is different from living it personally.
  • GAD involves more than ordinary worry.
  • Recovery requires patience, compassion, and persistence.
Source: adobe free stock by Lightfield Studios

As a therapist with over forty years of experience in the mental health field, I have come across clients presenting with anxiety on countless occasions. From education, workshops, conferences, and direct client contact, I’ve always felt I had a strong understanding of what their experiences were like.

A recent return of my own generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), the first instance being several years back preceding my cancer diagnosis, has reminded me of how little one can ever truly understand of the experience unless they've had the disorder themself.

Clinically, GAD is defined as “an anxiety disorder characterized by persistent, excessive, and difficult-to-control worry about multiple areas of life, such as health, work, family, finances, or everyday responsibilities.” In layman’s terms, GAD is the mother of all worries, which can weave its way into every aspect of life

Beyond the casual “worry” about one’s finances, employment, social conditions, and how one’s stock is doing, GAD’s version of worry typically:

  • Occurs more days than not for at least 6 months
  • Feels difficult to control
  • Is disproportionate to the actual situation
  • Causes meaningful distress or interferes with daily functioning

As if that was not enough, it’s also associated with at least 3 of these symptoms in adults:

  • Becoming tired easily
  • Difficulty concentrating or the mind going blank
  • Irritability
  • Muscle tension
  • Sleep problems
  • Restlessness or feeling keyed up

For myself, and many of the clients I’ve seen, there is a gradual buildup to these symptoms rather than all of them simply showing up one day. This downward spiral, also seen in many who struggle with depression, adds to the tension as one senses what is happening but feels helpless against its gravitational pull.

Early theories of anxiety pointed to excessive stress as the culprit. We now know that it arises from a complex series of experiences, genetics, and learned behavior that turns on the stress alarm system in the central nervous system (CNS) even when no threat is present. Over time, the CNS becomes dysregulated and needs very little to set it off.

Common contributors to GAD include:

  • Genetics
  • Brain and nervous-system sensitivity
  • Temperament
  • Chronic stress
  • Trauma or significant life experiences
  • Learned worry
  • Medical conditions and substances

To those of us who suffer from this condition (and suffer is truly the correct word), the search for relief can become a full-time experience. While cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), with or without medication support, is offered as an evidence-based best practice, it seldom has the quick relief that an anxious person desires. The wait for medications to build up to therapeutic levels and the wading through one’s psyche to find the sparks that lit the anxiety fire can feel exhausting.

To assist with the patience necessary to treat something as insidious as GAD, many like me turn to alternative methods of comfort and relaxation. Breathwork, yoga, Qi Gong, Reiki, prayer, mantras, or worry stones rubbed into a fine powder are just some of the techniques employed to stay afloat while being flooded with worst-case scenarios.

During my first go-round, my car was essentially a new age shop on wheels. I had worry stones, aromatherapy items, and printed reminders that “this too shall pass” stuck on my dashboard, prayer cards, and, harkening back to my Catholic upbringing, a rosary. I sought assistance through a trusted psychiatrist for medication, underwent hypnotherapy, read any book that seemed to promise an end to a racing mind, practiced mindfulness, yoga, and the not-so-subtle art of doing ordinary things even when my anxious mind said I couldn’t pull it off.

I wish I could say with certainty which of these techniques pulled me through and brought an end to the unending whirring of both body and mind—that way I would simply repeat the process and be typing these words with much calmer fingers.

I’ve met many clients through the years who, thinking they had conquered their inner demons, returned to counseling with the simple words, “It’s back.” The despair was palpable, and the first order of business was to remove any sense of guilt or shame for having brought this back into his or her life. Compassion is the key element for a wound that is already open and needs time to heal.

Equally important is to seek out those professionals who have a working knowledge of how a dysregulated nervous system responds to the world and who can act as a guide down the path of recovery—a recovery that is not about controlling the mind but retraining it to set off alarms when helpful and turn them off when not.

Much of GAD work takes place outside the provider’s office as we repeatedly practice the art and science of reconditioning our fight, flight, or freeze responses. Sometimes the task isn't to convince yourself that nothing bad will happen. It's learning that you don't need absolute certainty to keep living your life.

item.title: New Research on Gratitude
item.description:
Gratitude

New Research on Gratitude

How gratitude for our role models can bring us greater resilience and hope.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • New research shows gratitude can relieve stress, bring us positive emotions, and help us cope with challenges.
  • Acknowledging our role models and our gratitude for them can bring us greater resilience and hope.
  • We can find role models in parents, teachers, professional athletes, or anyone else who's inspired us

In these challenging times, new research shows how a gratitude practice can bring us greater resilience and well-being. Research participants who engaged in a gratitude practice for four weeks reported lower stress, increased positive emotions, and a greater ability to cope with challenging situations (Flores, et al., 2026).

Gratitude for Our Role Models

In this season of Thanksgiving, we can express gratitude for our role models, people who have inspired us by their example (Sariani & Nugraha, 2026). Research has long shown the benefits of gratitude and how much we are influenced by our role models (Bandura, 1986; Bricheno & Thornton, 2007; Emmons, 2007).

Recent studies show that we can find role models in our teachers and professional athletes (Obenda, 2026; Sariani & Nugraha, 2026). We can also find them in entertainers, and, for many of us, our first role models are our parents (Assibey-Mensah, 1997; Clark, Martin, & Bush, 2001).

With my dad, my first role model
Source: Diane Dreher photo

My First Role Model

My first role model was my father, Colonel Frank H. Dreher, who grew up on a small Kentucky farm during the Depression.

While working on the farm one afternoon, he saw a small plane flying overhead and ran to the local airport. Pilots would give a boy a quarter to help tie their plane down, and a quarter was a lot of money during the Depression.

When Frank reached the airport, a bright yellow biplane had just touched down. Inspired by its power and freedom, he knew he had to fly. Each day, after school, he’d return to the airport, helping the pilots tie down their planes, wash and refuel them. Sometimes they took him up on short flights. He did odd jobs around the airport and persevered to follow his dream. At age sixteen, he got his pilot’s license and was featured in the Louisville Courier-Journal as the youngest pilot in Kentucky.

My father became a flight instructor, a pilot during World War II, and an Air Force colonel who flew jets and air rescue helicopters. I’ve always admired him for his courage to soar high above the ground to follow his dreams (Dreher, 2025).

I’ve also been inspired by Eleanor Roosevelt, who had an unhappy childhood—constant criticism from her mother and an alcoholic father. Both parents died when she was a child, leaving her to be raised by her mother’s neglectful relatives. Yet she developed resilience and a heart of compassion, offering hope to so many people during the Depression and World War II. Her example inspires me to this day.

I’m also inspired by Jane Goodall. She grew up during World War II as a sensitive and curious child who loved nature. Climbing the tall tree beside her house, she dreamed of studying animals in Africa. She followed her curiosity and persevered. Her close observations of chimpanzees led to new scientific discoveries. And her love of nature led her to travel through the world, encouraging us to care for all the life on this beautiful planet.

Your Role Models

Who has been a role model for you?

Was it a parent, teacher, relative, or neighbor? Was it someone in history, someone in the news, or someone else?

If you feel grateful for this person, what are you thankful for?

What qualities about this person do you admire?

And how might you want to develop more of these qualities for yourself?

Acknowledging our role models and our gratitude for them can help us cope with our own life’s challenges with greater resilience and hope.

____________________________________

This post is for informational purposes and should not substitute for psychotherapy with a qualified professional.

item.title: How Do Borderline and Narcissism Differ?
item.description:
Personality Disorders

How Do Borderline and Narcissism Differ?

It is easier than you may think to learn to tell them apart.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Borderline PD and narcissistic PD both start in childhood as a reaction to family dynamics.
  • From an object relations theoretical viewpoint, borderline PD is a different disorder than narcissistic PD.
  • People with borderline PD get triggered by different things than people with narcissistic PD.
  • People with BPD want love and nurturing from partners, while people with NPD want admiration and respect .
Source: Nathan Cowley/Pexels

Although they may appear superficially similar, borderline personality disorder and narcissistic personality disorder are very different from each other. Although both develop similarly—a child with a particular inborn temperament tries to adapt to a parenting style that doesn't fit their needs—they diverge. The borderline adaptation focuses on getting love and nurturing and avoiding abandonment, while the narcissistic adaptation focuses on getting admiration and high status and avoiding being seen as flawed.

(In this post, I am using BPD and NPD, adaptations, and the terms borderline and narcissist as shorthand for someone who qualifies for a full diagnosis of borderline personality disorder or narcissistic personality disorder.)

What Do BPD and NPD Have in Common?

Both lack whole object relations and object constancy.

This means that people with BPD and NPD cannot form an integrated, realistic, and stable sense of themselves and other people. They can only shift back and forth between seeing themselves and other people as either all-good or all-bad.

The Split Object Relations Part Unit

A three-part unit forms when someone with a personality disorder interacts with others; however, it only shows one side of itself. Masterson called this a “split object relations part unit.” It comprises only good feelings or only bad ones.

Part 1—How the person with the PD feels about themself and acts.

Part 2—What the person with the PD believes the other person feels and thinks.

Part 3—The emotional atmosphere between them.

BPD Example: Carol and Her Husband’s Business Trip

Carol has borderline and severe abandonment issues from her childhood in foster care. Her husband, Bill, is leaving on a regularly scheduled business trip. Her old abandonment fears return when she sees him packing his suitcase. She knows he is traveling for business and will be back in three days, yet she becomes furious with him. She accuses him of not caring about her feelings and keeps him up half the night arguing.

Part 1-Carol’s View of Self: Unwanted and unlovable.

Part 2-Carol’s View of the Other: An abandoning, rejecting parent.

Part 3-Atmosphere: Poisoned by Carol’s hurt and anger.

NPD Example: Dave and the Dishwasher

Dave is a very controlling narcissist married to Callie. They divided their responsibilities. She gave up work to have their children and run the house, while he focused on earning enough money for their lifestyle. But Dave keeps picking fights over trivial household details. He kept Callie up half the night fighting because he felt disrespected when she rejected his suggestions of how she should load the dishwasher.

Part 1-Dave’s View of Self: Disrespected.

Part 2-Dave’s View of the Other: Acting superior to shame him.

Part 3-Atmosphere: Poisoned by Dave’s hatred and desire for revenge.

Benefits of the Object Relations Approach

People with BPD or NPD often sabotage important intimate relationships when they get emotionally triggered. The trigger is usually something associated with traumatic childhood experiences. Their reactions become more understandable when we look at their rage and splitting through an object relations lens. They are not really fighting with the actual person in front of them. This person has become an unconscious symbol of someone from their past who hurt them.

Once you understand the limitations that a lack of whole object relations imposes on intimate relationships, it is easier to understand why these relationships fail or are filled with ugly and unnecessary fights (Masterson, 1976; 1981). Here are some different versions one might encounter.

BPD Form of All-Good: I am lovable, and you love me, and we are feeling great right now. You are my good mommy or daddy. You will never do anything bad to me.

BPD Form of All-Bad: I am ugly and unlovable, and you are rejecting and abandoning me. You are my bad mommy or daddy.

NPD Form of All-Good: I am perfect, special, and entitled to the best of everything. You are my admiring audience who mirrors my perfection back to me. I feel great.

NPD Form of All-Bad: I am worthless, defective garbage. You are attacking and humiliating me. I feel deep shame and fear public humiliation.

People With Personality Disorders Lose Object Constancy During a Fight

If we have object constancy, we do not get as mean during a fight. We can remember things we like about our partner and our past good history together. If we lack object constancy, we lose touch with everything good when we feel hurt, disappointed, or angry with our partner.

Even if your lover with NPD or BPD declared their undying love for you 10 minutes ago, once he or she gets angry, their love turns to hatred.

Part of Carol’s problem with Bill leaving on a work trip is that she lacks object constancy and cannot feel her emotional connection to Bill (or his to her) when he is not at home with her. And her lack of it made it easier to abuse Bill because everything good about him was out of her awareness when she split on him the night before he left.

They Attribute Their Feelings to Other People

When they feel good in your presence, they project all good things onto you. When they feel unhappy, they blame you. Sometimes the all-good role is projected onto one person and all the split-off bad things are projected onto someone else.

BPD Example: Jane sees a psychiatrist for medication and a psychologist for psychotherapy. She splits and sees her therapist as her hero and her psychiatrist as her enemy.

NPD Example: Catherine treats her son as her “golden child,” while making her daughter into the family scapegoat.

Both Can Be Impulsive

People with BPD or NPD can get overly caught up in their current emotional state. They do things they later regret because they act impulsively and do not stop to think through the likely consequences.

BPD Example: Tanya got triggered by her new lover not texting her “good night” and impulsively blocked him on social media because she became convinced that he was cheating on her. He decided he did not want drama and broke up with her.

NPD Example: Married Harry ended up in therapy trying to save his marriage because his wife caught him having an affair with a pretty intern at work. Her attention had made him feel special.

What Are the Major Differences Between BPD and NPD?

Interpersonal Goals

BPD: Get unconditional love and nurturing from a combination lover/parent figure.

NPD: Gain high status, be acknowledged as special, all-knowing, and always right.

Interpersonal Fears

BPD: Being abandoned or engulfed by the emotional needs of the other person.

NPD: Experiencing a humiliating public failure that exposes them as flawed.

Summary

People with borderline personality disorder and people with narcissistic personality disorder sometimes behave in a similar fashion. But when you look closely, it is obvious that they are very different diagnoses. The disorders create different types of vulnerabilities, and people with BPD or NPD want different things from their partners and get triggered by different types of events. Think of a pear and an apple. They are both fruit, but most people can easily tell them apart if they have experience with both.

item.title: Love Perseveres: Grieving the Changes in Relationship Roles
item.description:
Grief

Love Perseveres: Grieving the Changes in Relationship Roles

Grief helps us recognize and eventually adapt to changes in relationships.

Posted November 11, 2026

Key points
  • Grief can mark changing relationship roles, not just the death of someone we love.
  • Grieving helps us recognize change and adapt to new ways of relating.
  • Normal life transitions can still hurt; love and self-compassion help us navigate them.

“But what is grief, if not love persevering?” (Donney & Shakman, 2021).

It is a famous line from Marvel Studios’ Disney+ series, WandaVision. Ironically, when I first encountered it while watching the series many years ago, I did not think much of it. I might have even rolled my internal eyes in response, thinking that it sounded good, but I had trouble appreciating that the statement could have any meaningful connection to my life.

I heard the same line again a few days ago in the new Marvel Studios’ Disney+ series, VisionQuest. And this time around, it landed differently.

I had always thought that this line was about death and coping with its aftermath. That’s the context under which Vision delivers the words of comfort to Wanda, who is trying to make sense of her brother’s death.

But my understanding of grief—specifically, what kinds of things in life can be grieved—has expanded over time. Grief certainly includes grappling with death, but it is not a process reserved for only interpersonal loss. From this perspective, Vision’s words struck an emotional chord.

I like to think of grief as first recognizing a shift or development, and then taking appropriate action based on the changes. That is, grief helps me to acknowledge that a change has arrived in my life, often abruptly; grief also helps me to adapt to the new reality. “Love persevering” speaks especially to this idea that accepting and making sense of changes can be incredibly difficult, but it is a worthwhile process because of love.

Here is another way to say it: grieving means that you care deeply about something, or someone.

In the rest of this blog post, I wish to focus on grieving the changes in relationship roles. As someone who can be described as part of a sandwich generation in life, in a real sense, I grieve the changes that I observe in the relationships that I have with my children and my aging father. To be clear, the shifts that I will reference are part of normal human development. But just because these are shared human experiences does not make them any easier to go through. Let me give two specific examples.

The other day, my teen daughter prepared a lunchbox and left it in the refrigerator for me to take to work. When I discovered this unexpected gift in the morning, I felt pride, joy, and all the other warm feelings that a parent might have in these unexpected moments of kindness from our own offspring. But at a higher level, I also felt a pang of sadness in being reminded that my baby is no longer a baby (and has not been for a long time!), and that she has entered into a different developmental phase. More specifically, her relationship with me, including the roles that we occupy in the relationship, has shifted.

And then there is my aging father. The combination of his strong personality and Korean cultural emphasis on elevating the paternal role meant that for most of my life, I related to my father in a vertical way, by honoring his preferences and seeing him as the sole decision-maker in the family. But now, as a man in his mid-40s, I see the role shift reflected in many areas of our relationship. Some changes are really acute, directly correlated with declining biology; he can’t read any fine print, so I read it for him. Other changes are more subtle, such as when the hospital worker becomes exasperated, turns to me, and asks that I explain what they are trying to say to my father.

Grief, in sitting with the real changes in front of us; then adaptation, in living into this new space of relating to each other differently.

Are you grieving the changes in your life, especially the interpersonal changes in people that you love? I pray that your love for that person will carry you through the process, even if it's difficult and requires much perseverance. And I hope that through it all, you can find ways to be compassionate to yourself and recognize that these are normal emotions and processes.
